sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Platte County, Missouri?
sections.html:
Three county offices share the work. The Assessor, Marcus Farr, values property. The County Clerk builds the tax book and takes Board of Equalization appeals and tax credit applications. The Collector of Revenue, Sheila L. Palmer, mails and collects the bills.

The Collector is in the Administration Building at 415 3rd St., Room 212, Platte City, MO 64079, phone (816) 858-3356, with the counter staffed on weekdays from 8 to 5. The Assessor's real estate staff answer at (816) 858-3316 until 4:30 in the afternoon. The County Clerk's number for tax relief questions is (816) 858-3340. The collector's FAQ sends questions about value, names, addresses, vehicles and tax waivers to the assessor, and questions about missing statements to the collector.

sections.h2: What makes Platte County different for a home seller?
sections.html:
Platte County is part of the Kansas City metro area, and the Missouri River forms its southwestern border with Kansas. The county was organized on December 31, 1838, out of the Platte Purchase, and Platte City is the seat. Kansas City International Airport lies inside the county, and other towns include Parkville, Weston, Riverside, Dearborn and Smithville.

Four public school systems serve the county: Park Hill, Platte County School District Number 3 at Platte City, North Platte R-I at Dearborn and West Platte County R-II at Weston. The Census Bureau's latest figures show the highest home values of the three Missouri counties in this guide set.

  • 114,400 residents in the 2025 estimate, a gain of 7.2 percent over the 2020 base.
  • 47,969 housing units, about two thirds occupied by their owners (67.4 percent).
  • A typical owned home is valued at $345,100 for the 2020 to 2024 period.
  • Median household income reaches $96,227, and gross rent runs $1,334 a month.
  • The county issued 425 building permits in 2025.

Source: Census QuickFacts.

sections.h2: When are Platte County tax bills due?
sections.html:
Platte County statements are mailed in November and are due on receipt. They become delinquent after December 31, and the assessor's calendar also lists November 1 as the day bills go out through the Collector. To avoid penalty and interest, the envelope must be postmarked on or before December 31. Anything postmarked later comes back unprocessed unless the penalty and interest are added.

The Collector states that a statement that never arrives does not remove the obligation, and that trouble with the phone or web payment system does not extend the statutory deadline. Check the mailing address and legal description on each bill. If you did not get a statement by the end of November, call the office right away.

sections.h2: How can I pay my Platte County bill?
sections.html:
The Collector accepts payment in person, by mail, online, by telephone using the 1-800 number printed on the bill, or through a 24-hour drop box outside the Platte County Government Complex. In the office, cash, personal check, cashier's check, money order and credit or debit card are accepted.

The drop box helps when the counter is closed. The Assessor's page lists county closures on November 26 and 27 and December 24 and 25 this year, so plan year-end payments around those days and ask the Collector for its own holiday schedule.

sections.h2: How does the 2027 reassessment affect Platte County owners?
sections.html:
Missouri law has the assessor reassess all real property on January 1 of each odd-numbered year, and Platte County's 2027 round is already underway. The assessor's FAQ says the aim is equalization, not extra revenue. Early estimates in that FAQ put about 8,000 parcels on track for a decrease, about 900 for an increase under 1 percent, and just under 13,000 for an increase over 15 percent.

A parcel projected to rise more than 15 percent, excluding new construction, gets a written notice and an exterior inspection. An interior look happens only if the owner asks for it. Estimated 2027 values appear on the assessor's Beacon property search beside the current 2026 value, and the assessor says they may change before final values are set in early 2027.

Assessment rates are 19 percent of market value for residential, 32 percent for commercial and 12 percent for agricultural property. A $50,000 home, as the assessor's own example shows, would carry an assessed value of $9,500. Source: Platte County Assessor, Real Property.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Platte County value?
sections.html:
The assessor lays out three steps, and each has its own date. Start with the informal review, then use the county board, then the state.

Platte County real property appeal steps listed by the assessor
StepWhereTiming
Informal hearingAssessor's appraisers, (816) 858-3316Before June 30
Board of EqualizationForm from the County ClerkReturned before the second Monday in July; hearings in July
State Tax CommissionComplaint for Review of AssessmentBy September 30, or 30 days after the board's decision if later

Bring pictures, a recent sale of your property or an appraisal to the informal meeting. An increase notice must be mailed on or before June 15. If you plan to pay under protest, the State Tax Commission guide says to pay in full by December 31, mark the check "paid under protest" and file a written statement with the collector.

sections.h2: What relief programs apply in Platte County?
sections.html:
The assessor's newsletter describes two county-run credits, both handled by the County Clerk and neither one a freeze on value. SB-190 is the senior tax credit, which protects a qualifying participant's base-year tax liability. SB-3, the Homestead Tax Credit enacted in April 2026, targets owner-occupied primary residences not already covered by SB-190 and limits yearly tax growth to 5 percent or the Consumer Price Index, whichever is greater. The newsletter says its full effect will show in the 2027 cycle.

Homes in either program are still reassessed, and a Greater Than 15% notice does not remove a participant from the credit. Call the County Clerk at (816) 858-3340 to ask about eligibility. The state Property Tax Credit claim is separate and pays up to $1,100 to qualifying owner-occupants who are seniors or 100 percent disabled (Missouri Department of Revenue).

sections.h2: What should a Platte County seller do about the tax bill?
sections.html:
Collect the latest bill or look up the parcel on the assessor's Beacon search before you list. The county sends a notice to the owner of record at the last address on file, so a seller who moved should file the assessor's change of address form to keep notices from being lost.

Confirm payoff figures with the Collector in Platte City, and ask the title company how the year will be divided at closing. The collector's statement is due on receipt, so a sale in November or December leaves little time between the bill arriving and the postmark deadline.

faqs.q: When do Platte County property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: They become delinquent after December 31. The envelope must be postmarked by that date, and later payments are returned unless penalty and interest are included.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Platte County property tax in person?
faqs.a: Go to the Collector's counter in the Administration Building at 415 3rd St., Room 212, Platte City, any weekday between 8 and 5. A 24-hour drop box sits outside the entrance to the government complex.

faqs.q: Did my Platte County value go up more than 15 percent?
faqs.a: Check the Assessor's Beacon search, which shows 2027 estimates beside the 2026 value. A projected increase over 15 percent, excluding new construction, triggers a mailed notice and an exterior inspection.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for a Platte County Board of Equalization appeal?
faqs.a: Return the form to the County Clerk before the second Monday in July. The assessor also asks owners to meet an appraiser informally before June 30.

faqs.q: Does the SB-3 Homestead Tax Credit freeze my Platte County home value?
faqs.a: No. SB-3 limits tax growth on an eligible primary residence to 5 percent or the CPI, whichever is greater, and homes in the program are still reassessed. Ask the County Clerk at (816) 858-3340 about eligibility.
